sentences.text: The generic name Kunpengopterus combines a Chinese mythological fish-whale and a Greek word for wing.
The type species Kunpengopterus sinensis had an elongated head measuring 10.7 cm in length.
A low bony crest behind the eyes was elongated by cartilage and possibly extended to the back by a skin flap.
Kunpengopterus possessed a long, stiff tail.
The fifth toe of Kunpengopterus was long and strongly curved.

A second species, Kunpengopterus antipollicatus, was described by Xuanyu Zhou and colleagues in 2021, featuring an opposable thumb on the wing, a feature rare among non-mammals, which earned it the nickname "Monkeydactyl".
Fossil evidence includes preserved soft parts and remains of a possibly regurgitated fish.
A specimen nicknamed "Mrs T" was preserved with an egg impression between its thighs.
The animal laid eggs with a parchment-like, soft shell that were small relative to the mother's size, resembling modern reptiles more than birds.
The genus Kunpengopterus was named and described by Wang Xiaolin and colleagues in 2010.
The type species is known from an almost complete skeleton found in the Tiaojishan Formation in western Liaoning.
An additional specimen with a skull was referred to the genus in 2017.
Researchers suggest Kunpengopterus likely buried many small eggs and that juveniles could fly immediately after hatching.
Analysis of a counterplate suggests the animal had two active ovaries producing one egg at a time.
Kunpengopterus is classified within the family Wukongopteridae.
Kunpengopterus lived during the middle to late Jurassic in northeastern China.
The genus lived between 168.2 and 152.21 million years ago.
It is debated whether the egg-bearing specimen represents sexual dimorphism, as researchers suggest crest size may vary with age rather than sex.
